analysis.one_liner: Creates federal standby loans that backstop coal-to-liquid fuel plants when oil prices fall.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee or floor vote in the 110th Congress, despite 65 cosponsors and a July 2008 discharge petition that failed to force one.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have let the Department of Energy sign loan agreements with up to six coal-to-liquid fuel projects. When oil prices dropped below an agreed floor, the government would send the projects money; when prices rose, the projects could defer their loan repayments, with the government recapturing some upside through a profit-sharing arrangement above a ceiling. Projects had to capture their carbon dioxide and show lifecycle emissions no worse than conventional petroleum fuel, and at least one project had to be owned by small coal producers.
analysis.who_benefits: Coal producers and coal-to-liquids developers, who would get a federal loan program designed to make first-of-a-kind coal fuel plants financeable even when oil prices are low — the main historical obstacle to the technology. Small coal producers would be guaranteed a share, with one project reserved for them. Coal states would gain jobs tied to new plants.

how_it_helps.text: The Secretary of Energy could enter standby loan agreements with up to six qualifying coal-to-liquid (CTL) projects, providing direct federal loans disbursed whenever market fuel prices fell below an agreed minimum price.

During the loan's primary term, projects could defer repayment obligations in any quarter when prices stayed below the cap price, with deferred amounts amortized with interest later — protecting borrowers from oil-price volatility.

Projects had to capture and sequester their carbon dioxide and be certified by EPA as producing fuel with lifecycle CO2 emissions at or below those of the same fuel made from petroleum, a condition aimed at answering the technology's main environmental objection.
At least one of the six loans had to go to a project owned in part by two or more small coal producers, and the government could take profit-sharing payments when prices exceeded the cap price.

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers, who would fund the government's disbursements whenever oil prices fell below the floor and absorb the risk if the projects underperformed — the bill required an upfront payment estimated to cover the loan's federal cost, but that estimate depends on oil-price volatility assumptions. Communities and the climate would also bear the environmental footprint of an expanded coal-fuels industry, even with the carbon-capture conditions.

drawbacks.text: The program put the federal government on the hook whenever oil prices fell below the agreed minimum, a contingent liability whose size depended entirely on future oil prices — the very uncertainty the bill asked OMB to price into the projects' upfront payments.

By insulating coal-to-liquid plants from low oil prices, the bill would entrench a capital-intensive industry that competes with petroleum only when prices are high, potentially leaving taxpayers supporting plants that are uneconomic on their own.

Even with the carbon-parity certification requirement, the bill would deepen transportation's reliance on coal, and the cap-price structure limits how much of the upside the government could recapture when prices surge.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill included real guardrails — an upfront payment meant to cover the loan's cost to the government, profit-sharing above a price ceiling, and an EPA certification requiring lifecycle carbon emissions no worse than petroleum fuel. But the fundamental bargain was that taxpayers would absorb coal-fuel projects' losses in cheap-oil years in exchange for uncertain upside, to build an industry that has struggled to reach commercial scale. The environmental conditions narrowed, but did not eliminate, the climate cost of making transportation fuel from coal.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in two House subcommittees for over a year, a discharge petition filed to force a floor vote never gathered the 218 signatures needed, and it died when the 110th Congress ended in January 2009.

narrative.text: Rep. Rick Boucher (D-VA) introduced the bill on May 8, 2007, with nine original cosponsors, and it was referred to the Energy and Commerce and Science and Technology committees.
It was sent to the Energy and Air Quality Subcommittee in Energy and Commerce and the Energy and Environment Subcommittee in Science and Technology, where it stayed without any markup or vote.

On July 9, 2008, Rep. Peter Roskam (R-IL) filed a discharge petition (Petition No. 110-12) — a device that forces a bill to the floor if a majority of House members, 218, sign it — but the bill never reached the floor.
The bill expired when the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009, without either chamber ever voting on it.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, taxpayers avoided a contingent federal loan liability to coal-to-liquids projects, and no federal money was committed to an unproven coal fuel industry. Coal producers and developers who wanted the financing lost their chance; the bill's 65 cosponsors got no vote on it.

sides.party_line_note: Support was bipartisan but heavily Republican — 57 of the 65 cosponsors were Republicans, alongside Democratic sponsor Boucher and 8 Democratic cosponsors — while the Democratic-run committees that held the bill never acted on it, and no roll-call vote was ever taken.

industries.note: Federal loans that pay out when oil prices are low would make coal-to-liquid plants financeable, creating a new, guaranteed demand channel for coal. The public bears the loan risk and the climate footprint even with the bill's carbon-capture conditions.

The bill's entire purpose was to de-risk first-of-a-kind CTL plants, historically stalled by volatile oil prices and huge capital costs. Its price-floor disbursements and deferred repayments transfer that risk from developers to taxpayers.
The bill reserved at least one of six loan slots for a project owned by two or more small coal producers, giving them an assured path into the program.

industries.industry: Petroleum refiners and petroleum coke processors
industries.note: The bill allowed one qualifying project to convert refinery waste products, including petroleum coke, into fuel — a narrow new outlet for a refinery waste stream.
